sources: Interim financial statements to 31 Dec 2025, 31 Mar, 30 Jun and 30 Sep 2026

price.note: Closed Rs 140.00 on 30 September 2026; July–September range Rs 135.50–144.25; Q1 2026 high Rs 167.00.

summary.headline: Still growing well, but at Rs 157 the price is a little above fair value: wait for Rs 122 or lower
summary.text: Sampath Bank (SAMP.N0000) is a well-run bank that keeps growing, but at Rs 157 the price is a little above fair value. The September 2026 report showed group profit up 15% to Rs 26.5bn for nine months (EPS Rs 22.63 against Rs 19.74), with gross loans up 22% to Rs 1.5tn and Stage 3 loans down to 6.07%. It trades at 0.91x its group NAV of Rs 173.18 and 5.1x trailing earnings, with a 6.6% dividend yield. But a Sri Lankan bank needs a high return (I use an 18% cost of equity), and on that basis four methods put fair value at about Rs 144 (Rs 141 before, raised by the higher book value), so the price is about 9% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 122 and treat under Rs 108 as a strong buy. The trade-off is capital: CET1 fell to 12.27% from 14.75% in nine months as loans grew, so the bank raised Rs 10bn of Tier 2 debentures in October; costs are rising faster than income and impairments are up sharply.

valuation.note: Fair value weights the bear/base/bull averages of the four methods 30/50/20 (about 0.83x group NAV).

highlights.title: Nine months to September 2026 (group, unaudited)
highlights.text: Profit after tax rose 15% to Rs 26.5bn; EPS Rs 22.63 against Rs 19.74. Third-quarter profit rose 15% (bank 18%), so growth held up after the first half.

highlights.title: What drove it
highlights.text: Net interest income up 15% (margin 4.22%), fees up 21%, exchange income up 67% to Rs 5.9bn as the rupee weakened. Bond-sale gains fell to Rs 1.1bn from Rs 3.8bn. Tax fell 17% because prior-year assessments were finalised (a one-off).

highlights.title: Costs and provisions
highlights.text: Operating costs rose 22%, faster than income, so cost-to-income rose to 44.3% from 41.5%. Impairments on loans rose to Rs 8.1bn from Rs 2.3bn on Rs 273bn of loan growth and extra buffers, partly offset by a Rs 1.3bn reversal on foreign-currency bonds after Fitch upgraded Sri Lanka.

highlights.title: Loans, asset quality and capital
highlights.text: Gross loans grew 22% to Rs 1.50tn; deposits 13% to Rs 1.83tn. Gross Stage 3 fell to 6.07% (coverage 68.7%). CET1 fell to 12.27% and total capital to 15.32%; the bank raised Rs 10bn through Basel III debentures in October 2026, after a Rs 10bn green bond in July.

highlights.title: Presentation change
highlights.text: Recoveries of written-off loans are now netted within impairment charges, and last year's comparatives were reclassified to match. Profit isn't affected.

methodReadings.reading: Group NAV per share at 30 September 2026. The price is 0.91x NAV, so it passes your NAV rule.
On trailing group EPS of Rs 30.66. Bank year-end P/E: 5.7x (2025), 5.1x (2024), 4.8x (2023), 3.0x (2022).
Rs 10.30 cash for 2025 (40% of profit), paid once a year after the annual results.
Total capital 15.32%, down from 17.65% at end-2025 as loans grew 22%. Still above minimums; Rs 10bn of Tier 2 debentures raised in October.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: Values the bank as a multiple of its book value, set by long-run ROE against the cost of equity and growth.

models.name: P/E method
models.comment: The most generous method, because the base case assumes the market pays 5.5x earnings, close to its recent range.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: The strictest method, because the bank keeps 60% of its profit to fund loan growth instead of paying it out.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Used instead of a cash-flow DCF, which doesn't suit a bank: book value plus profit earned above the 18% required return.

modelsNote: A bank's cash flows are mostly lending and deposits, so instead of a cash-flow DCF I used residual income and a justified price-to-book, alongside P/E and dividends.

scenarios.common: Sri Lankan 7–10-year government bonds yield about 12% (November 2026), plus a premium for a leveraged bank with large government-bond holdings. Payout stays near 40%. Nine-month EPS is Rs 22.63, so 2026 EPS of about Rs 31 needs a fourth quarter similar to the third (Rs 7.40).

sensitivity.title: Residual income base case, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Today's Rs 157 needs a 16% cost of equity, or an 18% cost of equity with a long-run ROE above 17%.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 63,300 in total, against Rs 78,500 for 500 shares at Rs 157.
buyPlan.realism: The 2026 low so far is Rs 135.50 (July–September), and the 2025 low was Rs 99.90. Rs 144 needs about an 8% fall, which has happened this year; Rs 122 needs about 22%, which would need a broad market sell-off.

higher: Loan growth continuing while Stage 3 loans keep falling.
The net interest margin holding above 4.2%.
Lower interest rates, which would lower the cost of equity.
Cost growth slowing back below income growth.
lower: Capital being used up by fast loan growth, leading to smaller cash dividends, a scrip dividend or a rights issue (CET1 is already 12.27%).
A provisioning cycle as the 2026 loan growth seasons.
The tax settlement and exchange gains not repeating.
Costs rising faster than income (up 22% against 14%).
Higher taxes on banks in the budget.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the 2025 annual report and the 2025–2026 interim reports to September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, and the price is the CSE close of 12 November 2026, so check it before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

fullText:
Summary: Sampath Bank (SAMP.N0000) is a well-run bank that keeps growing, but at Rs 157 the price is a little above fair value. The September 2026 report showed group profit up 15% to Rs 26.5bn for nine months (EPS Rs 22.63 against Rs 19.74), with gross loans up 22% to Rs 1.5tn and Stage 3 loans down to 6.07%. It trades at 0.91x its group NAV of Rs 173.18 and 5.1x trailing earnings, with a 6.6% dividend yield. But a Sri Lankan bank needs a high return (I use an 18% cost of equity), and on that basis four methods put fair value at about Rs 144 (Rs 141 before, raised by the higher book value), so the price is about 9% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 122 and treat under Rs 108 as a strong buy. The trade-off is capital: CET1 fell to 12.27% from 14.75% in nine months as loans grew, so the bank raised Rs 10bn of Tier 2 debentures in October; costs are rising faster than income and impairments are up sharply.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 157.00, the CSE close on 12 November 2026. It closed September at Rs 140.00 after a July–September range of Rs 135.50–144.25.
Nine months to September 2026 (group, unaudited): profit after tax up 15% to Rs 26.5bn; EPS Rs 22.63 against Rs 19.74. Third quarter up 15%.
Drivers: net interest income up 15% (margin 4.22%), fees up 21%, exchange income up 67%; bond-sale gains down; costs up 22% (cost-to-income 44.3%); loan impairments Rs 8.1bn against Rs 2.3bn; tax down 17% on prior-year settlements.
Balance sheet: gross loans Rs 1.50tn (up 22%), deposits Rs 1.83tn, gross Stage 3 6.07% (coverage 68.7%), CET1 12.27%, total capital 15.32%. Rs 10bn of Basel III debentures raised in October 2026.
2025 (group): profit Rs 32.6bn, EPS Rs 27.77, dividend Rs 10.30, NAV Rs 165.23.

Valuation table (Rs per share)
Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted
Justified price to book | 115.5 | 158.7 | 218.8 | 157.8
P/E | 130.5 | 170.5 | 208.0 | 166.0
Dividend model | 71.3 | 106.4 | 147.6 | 104.1
Residual income | 101.4 | 148.9 | 215.1 | 147.9
Average | 104.7 | 146.1 | 197.4 | 144

What changed
Book value rose to Rs 173.18 from Rs 166.78, lifting the price-to-book and residual-income methods. With nine months known, I narrowed 2026 EPS to Rs 29 / 31 / 32 (from 28 / 31 / 33). Fair value Rs 141 → Rs 144, buy Rs 120 → Rs 122, strong buy Rs 106 → Rs 108.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity 20% / 18% / 16.5%; long-run ROE 15% / 17% / 19%; ROE path 16.5%→14% / 18%→16% / 19%→18%; growth 5% / 6% / 7%; 2026 EPS 29 × 4.5 / 31 × 5.5 / 32 × 6.5; dividends Rs 11.00, 4% / Rs 12.40, 7% / Rs 13.20, 9%.

Business tests: 4 of 4 passed; a good business at a slightly high price: watch list.

500-share plan
200 shares up to Rs 144, 150 up to Rs 122, 150 up to Rs 108: about Rs 63,300 in total.

quality.reason: A strong bank: good returns, sound capital and a high dividend.
